paras: The attempted lynching of Harvey Williams took place at Bramwell, West Virginia, on March 27-28, 1903, when a crowd gathered to lynch Williams, a Black coal miner jailed on a charge of assaulting a 13-year-old white girl. Officers took him out of the jail in plain clothes and moved him to Princeton, and the crowd then tore the Bramwell jail apart and fired hundreds of shots into the air. The story ran as a wire item across the country, and a list of the year's mob cases later recorded a hanging at Bluefield on March 29.

Williams worked for the Mill Creek Coal and Coke Company, lived at Coopers with his wife and family less than 100 yards from the Jones home, and came from Tazewell, Virginia. The Alexandria Gazette gave his age as 45. According to a Bluefield special telegram, he had spent the previous night and day drinking at Pocahontas and was walking home when the alleged assault took place.

Williams was accused of assaulting the daughter of a white miner named Jones, given as Mary or May, on the mountain path between Pocahontas, Virginia, and Coopers, and leaving her for dead. The girl reached home and gave the alarm, and within half an hour several posses were searching for him. Officers caught him in the mountains near Pocahontas, or at work in his garden according to the Clinch Valley News, and lodged him in the jail at Bramwell.

That night the jail was 'heavily guarded' while, by the Alexandria Gazette's account, people crowded into the village 'from all sections of the coal field'. The first dispatch said information from Bramwell pointed to 'a lynching and probably a burning before daylight'. After dark, with hundreds assembled 'bent on lynching' him, officers in citizens' clothes led Williams through the crowd and took him to the jail at Princeton, the county seat, ten miles away.
Believing he was still inside, the crowd made 'an onslaught' on the Bramwell jail and left it 'practically torn to pieces'. On finding him gone, the crowd fired hundreds of pistol shots into the air.

The Clinch Valley News expected no second attempt, since the Princeton jail was among the strongest in the state. No report of arrests in the crowd, or of an indictment or trial of Williams, was found in the coverage, and the girl's fate after reports that she was in serious condition is not recorded.

The first wire, datelined Bluefield on March 27, appeared under the Wichita Daily Eagle's headline 'Lynching of Negro Who Assaulted White Girl, Is Likely' and in the Indianapolis Journal. In West Virginia the Wheeling Register headed its special telegram 'Black Fiend Ravashes Little Girl' and predicted a lynching, though it added that Williams had 'conducted himself very properly' before. The March 28 wire ran on March 29 in Indianapolis, Wheeling, Louisville and Savannah under headlines such as 'Negro Spirited Away' and 'Tore Jail Down to Lynch Negro'.

These accounts stated the assault as fact and called Williams 'the brute', describing a mob 'Cheated of Contemplated Prey', while the Courier-Journal's headline called him a 'Negro Accused of Criminal Assault'. The Clinch Valley News, a Virginia weekly near the scene, titled its account 'An Awful Crime' but closed by noting his good reputation. Weekly digests in Vermont, West Virginia and North Dakota reduced the episode to a single line about a jail torn apart and a narrow escape; no account in the Black press was found.

A 'Mob Law' list printed on July 1 in Kentucky and Oklahoma papers recorded 'Negro hanged, Bluefield, W. Va., March 29' without a name. Every report from the week of the event, including those from West Virginia and nearby Virginia, says Williams was removed to Princeton before the crowd broke into the jail. Reports also differ on whether the jail was attacked about midnight or about 11 o'clock the next morning.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Harvey Williams
bases: A crowd gathered at Bramwell to lynch Harvey Williams, a Black miner held on an assault accusation, and tore the jail apart after officers had removed him (A5, A6, A12); it is an attempted lynching.

Contemporary reports agree that Williams was taken to the Princeton jail before 'hundreds of people' attacked the Bramwell jail, so no one was killed (A5, A6, A10, A12); only two unnamed July lists record a 'Negro hanged, Bluefield, W. Va., March 29' (A15, A16), which no March or April report supports. It was an attempted lynching.

The Mar 27 wire (A1), the Wheeling Register's special telegram (A4), the Mar 28 wire (A5, A6) and the Clinch Valley News (A12) agree on the accusation, the jailing at Bramwell, the removal to Princeton and the mob's wrecking of the jail; later lists that say a hanging took place (A15, A16) conflict only on the outcome.

accounts.label: Mar 27 wire
accounts.gist: Williams assaulted the girl and left her for dead; posses caught him near Pocahontas; the guarded Bramwell jail was expected to see 'a lynching and probably a burning before daylight'.

accounts.label: Wheeling Register special telegram
accounts.gist: Adds his employer, family and Tazewell origin and says he had been drinking at Pocahontas and 'conducted himself very properly' before.

accounts.label: Mar 28 wire
accounts.gist: Officers in plain clothes led Williams through the crowd to Princeton; the crowd later wrecked the Bramwell jail and fired hundreds of shots in the air.

accounts.label: Clinch Valley News
accounts.gist: Officers found him at work in his garden; a mob broke open the jail Friday night; the strong Princeton jail made another attempt unlikely.

accounts.label: July 'Mob Law' list
accounts.gist: Lists 'Negro hanged, Bluefield, W. Va., March 29' among the year's mob cases, without a name.

framing.detail: The Mar 27 wire, headed 'Lynching of Negro Who Assaulted White Girl, Is Likely', stated the assault as fact and forecast a lynching and burning without comment.
The Wheeling Register's headline called Williams a 'Black Fiend' and said lynching was expected 'to avenge foul crime', but the story noted his good conduct before.
The Mar 28 wire called him 'the brute' and the mob 'Cheated of Contemplated Prey', while the Courier-Journal's headline credited officers with saving a 'Negro Accused'.
Digest papers reduced it to one line that he 'narrowly escaped lynching'; July lists counted a Bluefield hanging.

versions.value: Removed to Princeton before the mob attacked; not harmed

conflicts.note: The contemporary dispatches, including West Virginia and nearby Virginia papers, are better evidence than an unsourced list compiled three months later; the list may count this episode as a hanging in error.

versions.value: Mar 27 ('to-day' in a Mar 27 dispatch; 'last Friday')

conflicts.note: The Alexandria Gazette's 'yesterday afternoon' in a Mar 28 issue fits Mar 27.

record_check.dossier: Harvey Williams only; Mary Jones is the girl he was accused of assaulting, not a target of the mob.
He was in custody and the mob attacked the jail to take him, but officers had already removed him to Princeton; he was not taken.
Posses caught him; the attackers were a mob of 'hundreds of people'.
Shots were fired into the air, not at anyone; the jail was wrecked.

record_check.record: Ends with crowds gathering and a report he would be lynched
record_check.dossier: Should add that officers took him to Princeton and the mob tore the Bramwell jail to pieces.
No paper names the county; Princeton is 'the county seat'.

info: Assault alleged Mar 26 or 27, 1903 ('to-day' in a Mar 27 dispatch; 'Thursday morning' in the Clinch Valley News; 'last Friday' in the Shepherdstown Register); crowd gathered the night of Mar 27 and wrecked the jail that night or about 11 a.m. Mar 28.
Assault alleged on the mountain between Pocahontas, Va., and Coopers, W. Va.; Williams jailed at Bramwell, W. Va., where the crowd attacked the jail; removed to the jail at Princeton, ten miles away.
Harvey Williams, a Black ('negro') coal miner, 45 years old per one report, employed by the Mill Creek Coal and Coke Company, living at Coopers, married, from Tazewell, Va.
Accused of assaulting ('outraged', 'criminally assaulted') a 13-year-old white girl, named Mary Jones (A1, A3) or May Jones (A4), daughter of a miner, and leaving her for dead.
A crowd of local people gathered at Bramwell 'from all sections of the coal field'; no one was named.
0 in contemporary reports; two July lists record a 'Negro hanged, Bluefield, W. Va., March 29'.
Williams was held in the Princeton jail; the Clinch Valley News expected no further attempt on him. No report of an indictment or trial was found.
